coverage: Stromboli and Eyjafjallajökull so far; the observatory’s pages are read for each volcano as its profile is rebuilt, and its current statement on activity is recorded on the page with the date
sample_note: Stromboli: highest point about 926 m, crater terrace at about 700–750 m, base about 2,000 m below sea level, explosions minutes to hours apart, strongest paroxysms 1919, 1930, 2003, 2019, ages of about 200,000 and 85,000 years. Eyjafjallajökull (read 2026-11-17): IMO page: most recent eruption 2010, about 25 km west of Katla, ice-filled caldera about 2.5 km wide; ICAO report: flank eruption 20 Mar–12 Apr 2010, summit eruption from 01:15 on 14 Apr under about 200 m of ice to 22 May (39 days), last activity 17 Jun, plume mostly 4–8 km and never above 10 km, tephra 0.27 km³, about 100,000 flights cancelled, two deaths from exposure, summit 1,651 m at Hámundur, ice cap about 80 km² above 800–900 m.
notes: Eyjafjallajökull: the IMO overview page gives the height as 1,666 m, the IMO-led report and the Smithsonian give 1,651 m: the page prints 1,651 m and mentions the other. The overview page also has "1921-1823" for the eruption of 1821–1823.

source: USGS volcano observatories: pages and fact sheets read per volcano (Mauna Loa: overview, FAQ, geology and history, 2022 eruption, Volcano Watch of 20 Aug 1998; Mount St. Helens: Fact Sheets 036-00 and 2005-3045, the 2004–2008 activity page; Kilauea: overview, Eruption Information, summit eruption FAQ, 2018 eruption and collapse, Geology and History, Fact Sheet 132-98, Volcano Watch of 28 Aug 2008 and 2 Jul 2026)
publisher: U.S. Geological Survey (Hawaiian and Cascades Volcano Observatories)
attribution: Source: U.S. Geological Survey, Hawaiian Volcano Observatory — retrieved Nov 2026
coverage: Mauna Loa, Mount St. Helens and Kilauea so far; the observatory pages of a US volcano are read when its profile is rebuilt
sample_note: Mauna Loa: summit 4,169 m (13,679 ft), threat potential very high, flanks about 5,000 m further down to the sea floor, sea floor pressed down about 8,000 m, more than 17,000 m base to summit, 34 eruptions since 1843, three since 1950, 38 years quiet from 1984 to 2022, first lava 0.6 to 1 million years ago, above the sea about 300,000 years ago, area about 5,100 km2, volume at least 75,000 km3, caldera 5 by 3.2 km, 2022 flows 19 km long and 2.8 km short of the highway. All five pages answer 200. Mount St. Helens (17 Nov 2026): summit 9,677 ft before and 8,363 ft after May 18, 1980; crater 1.2 by 1.8 miles and 2,084 ft deep; 57 deaths; landslide 0.67 cubic miles; blast 230 square miles; 2004–08 dome about 92 million m3; history about 300,000 years. All three pages answer 200. Kilauea (read 2026-11-17): summit 1,222 m (4,009 ft); eruption since 23 Dec 2024, episode 56 on 5 Nov 2026; tallest fountain 540 m (1,770 ft) in episode 43 on 10 Mar 2026; Halemaʻumaʻu floor 1,023 m before and 518 m after the 2018 collapse, lava surface 1,007 m on 30 Jun 2026; 2018: 35.5 sq km covered, 875 acres of new land, 62 collapses.
notes: The overview page gives the summit as 4,169 m, the FAQ as about 4,170 m: the page prints the overview figure. The FAQ says seven flows threatened Hilo and lists eight, and gives three different distances for the 1984 flow: the page prints no count and uses the list’s distance to Komohana Street. Mount St. Helens: USGS counts 57 deaths for May 18, 1980 and NOAA’s database lists 61; the page prints both and leads with USGS. Kilauea: the overview gives the summit as 1,222 m while the FAQ lists the Uēkahuna overlook on the rim at 1,247 m: the page prints both and says which is which. The Eruption Information page says the 2020–2023 eruptions filled about 410 m to an elevation of 910 m, which does not add up from 518 m: the page prints the elevations only. USGS calls its 2026 crater figures preliminary; the page says so. Episode counts change about every 11 days: the page gives them with their dates. Counts of buildings lost in 2018 differ between USGS pages (more than 700 structures, 716 dwellings, more than 724 structures): the page uses the 2018 science page. The quick-facts box still says the most recent eruption was June 2024.
